Please review the following manuscript. I've poured days of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util, os, shutil
for name in ['python3','pdftotext','pdftoppm','pdfinfo','gs','mutool']:
 print(name,shutil.which(name))
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
 print(name,importlib.util.find_spec(name))
print('runtime',os.listdir('/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/runtime/pdf'))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES:',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA:',r.metadata)
text=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(t)
 text.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(text))
print(''.join(text[:3]))
PY"
/bin/bash -c 'cat tmp/pdfs/page-18.txt tmp/pdfs/page-19.txt tmp/pdfs/page-20.txt tmp/pdfs/page-21.txt tmp/pdfs/page-22.txt tmp/pdfs/page-23.txt'

strengths: Combining label propagation or label spreading with a BORE-style acquisition function is a sensible, potentially useful contribution, particularly when a finite pool of unlabeled candidates is already available.

The evaluation includes synthetic functions, hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and MNIST embedding search, with 20 repetitions and standard errors. Figures 2, 3, and 6 show substantial improvements over several BORE/LFBO implementations, providing promising evidence for the proposed combination.

The appendices examine kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distributions, pool subsampling, and quantile thresholds. Including a control without unlabeled data and acknowledging cases where additional unlabeled points hurt performance are valuable.
The paper explains its relationship to TPE, BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised methods, and provides algorithms and search-space specifications that make the overall approach understandable.
weaknesses: The principal evidential gap is whether unlabeled-data propagation causes the reported gains. Figure 12 shows that the estimator without transductive learning can match or outperform SSL, notably on Bukin6 and on Branin with label spreading. However, this control uses fixed beta = 0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta. A comparably tuned Nadaraya–Watson baseline, evaluated across the main benchmarks with matched acquisition optimization and tie-breaking, is needed to distinguish the benefit of SSL from the kernel classifier, bandwidth selection, and randomized selection among maxima.

The proposed explanation for improved exploration is insufficiently supported. Assumption 4.1 relates input density to objective-derived labels; sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not establish that relationship, especially as the quantile threshold changes. Uniformly sampled pools also do not inherently satisfy it. Appendix D appropriately acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. theory does not apply, but its assertion that reducing a margin expands the favorable decision region does not establish better exploration or optimization. Targeted measurements of search coverage and behavior under violated cluster assumptions would strengthen this central claim.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: feature scaling for the Euclidean kernel, label-spreading alpha, propagation tolerance and iteration limit, beta optimization bounds and initialization, and several baseline training settings. The stated use of L-BFGS-B also needs a precise explanation for finite candidate pools, particularly MNIST embeddings, including admissible-candidate selection and handling of previously evaluated points. These choices can materially affect the comparisons.

The evidence has limitations beyond the tested settings. All continuous synthetic objectives are two-dimensional, while the 64-dimensional MNIST representation is trained on 440,000 labeled examples of the same digit-prediction task. The shared representation permits an internal comparison, but provides limited evidence for general high-dimensional black-box optimization. Random search would also provide a useful reference for the finite-pool tasks.

Computational practicality is incompletely assessed. The method repeatedly constructs a dense similarity graph, optimizes beta, and uses 1,000 acquisition-search initializations. Figure 14 usefully measures sensitivity to pool size, but does not compare total optimization overhead against BORE/LFBO under the main experimental settings. Consequently, the practical tradeoff between evaluation savings and additional computation remains unclear.

Smaller mathematical corrections are needed. The definition p_ij = w_ij / sum_k w_kj implies P = W D^{-1} for the symmetric kernel, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W before applying P transpose in Equation 11. Definition D.1 also introduces C_0 and C_1 but subsequently uses C_1 and C_2. These inconsistencies should be resolved against the actual implementation.
